findings.title: build() ignores new `limit` param; always returns 10 items
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `limit=10` to the public module-level function `build`, whose name/signature promises to cap the number of generated results (the default 10 even mirrors the existing cap). The body still hardcodes `max_count = 10` and iterates `range(max_count)`, never reading `limit`. A caller invoking `build('x', limit=3)` receives 10 items, not 3 — the promised capping behavior directly affects the data the caller receives, so the contract is broken even with no in-repo caller yet.

findings.title: New public `limit` param is ignored; body still hardcodes 10
findings.whyItBreaks: `build` is a public (non-underscore) module-level function, so its signature is the contract. Adding `limit=10` promises the caller can cap how many items are returned, but the body still sets `max_count = 10` on line 2 and never reads `limit`. Any caller passing e.g. `build('p', 3)` gets 10 elements — a silent wrong result (over-production) with no error. This is not a no-op optional parameter: the name `limit` explicitly promises result capping, which is behavior a caller observes in the returned data.

findings.title: Honor or remove unused `limit` param in build()
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed signature advertises a cap of `limit` (default 10), but the body computes `max_count = 10` (src/builder.py:2) and loops `range(max_count)` (src/builder.py:4), ignoring `limit` entirely. Any caller passing `limit=3` (or any value != 10) receives 10 items, so the promised capping is not implemented and the parameter is a dead second source of truth for the count. The default matching 10 masks the bug for callers relying on the default.

findings.title: Rename promises positive-int validation the body never performs
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int is a public module-level carrier whose name asserts validation/capping of the value, but the body is still just `return int(value)` — zero and negative inputs are accepted (parse_positive_int('-5') -> -5, parse_positive_int('0') -> 0). This is not dead: charge at src/validators.py:6 reads it and multiplies straight through, so charge('-5') -> -500 and total_cents(['-5']) -> -500, emitting a negative charge/total. Any caller that (reasonably) skips its own positivity check because of the name receives an unvalidated, wrong-signed value; the promised behavior (validation) is exactly what Trigger C flags as affecting the result a caller receives.

findings.title: Widened value type but body reads .length, undefined for numbers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported FieldProps contract now promises value may be a number (line 2), but the body computes `value.length` (line 6). Numbers have no `length` property, so for any number argument the template literal interpolates undefined and the input renders the literal string 'len=undefined' instead of a meaningful label. It is also a TypeScript compile error: TS2339 Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'. Previously the string-only type rejected numeric callers at the type level; the widening removes that guard without adding handling.

findings.title: Widening value to string|number breaks .length access
findings.whyItBreaks: The interface now promises callers may pass a number (`value: string | number` @src/components/Field.tsx:2), but the body reads `value.length` @src/components/Field.tsx:6. Under TypeScript this fails to compile (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'`), so any consumer project build breaks; if the type error is bypassed (e.g. non-strict/JS), a number has no `.length`, so `value.length` is `undefined` and the rendered label becomes the literal `len=undefined` instead of the intended length. Either way a number input can never produce a correct result.

findings.title: value.length is undefined for the newly-allowed number values
findings.whyItBreaks: The public `FieldProps.value` type was widened to `string | number`, promising callers may pass numbers, but the body computes `value.length`. `Number` has no `length`, so at runtime `value.length` is `undefined` and the label becomes the literal `len=undefined`; TypeScript also rejects the union member (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'`), so a typed build fails. The new promise (accept numbers) is not implemented by the body.

findings.title: Input now renders len=N instead of the field value
findings.whyItBreaks: `defaultValue` was changed from the prop `value` to a derived debug string. The component's observable output is now `len=<n>` (and `len=undefined` for numbers) rather than the caller-supplied value, so any consumer that displays or pre-fills this input shows wrong content — a user-facing regression independent of the number-widening.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer: >1 MiB diffs now fail the review
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is the only transport for the full PR patch (git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha]) at :140) and the changed-file list (:141 → git(["diff","--name-only",...]) at :57). Removing maxBuffer reverts spawnSync to Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes; when the diff exceeds 1 MiB Node terminates the child and sets error ENOBUFS with status null, so the `res.status !== 0` check at :38 throws `git diff ... failed:` (with an empty stderr, since the real cause is res.error, not stderr). runGithub() then takes the catch path (:182-194), posts a failing check-run and exits 1 — the review workflow breaks for any PR whose patch is larger than 1 MiB, which previously worked at 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer; large diffs now abort the whole review
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer drops the limit to Node's spawnSync default of 1 MiB. git() is used at line 140 for the full `git diff mergeBase headSha` patch and relies on the removed 64 MiB ceiling. On any PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync truncates stdout and sets res.error with res.status === null, so `res.status !== 0` (line 38) throws `git ... failed:` with the truncated/empty stderr. That throw happens at lines 138-141, i.e. BEFORE the try/catch at line 176, so runGithub rejects, no postCheck/postReview runs, and the PR gets no Needlefish check-run at all. If a Node version instead returns status 0 with truncated stdout, the truncated patch is silently used as the review input. Either way large PRs regress versus the previous 64 MiB behavior.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer in git() or large PR diffs abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: `spawnSync` defaults `maxBuffer` to 1 MiB, and this same helper runs `git diff mergeBase headSha` (line 140) to build the entire patch the reviewer consumes. Any PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated code, vendored files — easily >10 MiB) makes git exit non-zero with ENOBUFS, so line 38 throws, runGithub's catch posts a `failure` check ("Review errored and did NOT pass this PR"), and process.exitCode=1. The other helpers still carry `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` (lines 19, 29), confirming the limit was deliberate; only `git()` was reduced.

findings.title: Bundle.baseSha now reports the base tip, not the diff's merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: The shorthand `baseSha` is not the value previously stored: it is `process.env.PR_BASE_SHA` (the base branch tip, line 138), whereas `patch` (line 140) and `changedFiles` (line 141) are computed from `mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha` (line 139). Whenever PR_BASE_SHA is set and the base branch advanced after the PR branch forked — the normal case for any PR against a moving main — `mergeBase != baseSha`, so the Bundle advertises a base SHA that contains commits outside the diff it ships. Consumers of bundle.baseSha (review/prompt/metadata; the module is imported from ../core/review, which is not present in this checkout) now see a base that is inconsistent with bundle.patch and bundle.changedFiles, i.e. a wrong base/range for the review.

findings.title: Zero-valued runner duration override is silently replaced by fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs previously accepted an explicit 0 (`parsed >= 0`) and returned 0; the new `parsed > 0` reclassifies 0 as invalid and returns fallbackMs. That value is the duration handed to setTimeout on the shutdown path: RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS at line 124 (SIGTERM→SIGKILL escalation) and RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS at line 123 (post-SIGKILL give-up wait). So `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` or `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0`, which previously meant an immediate (0ms) transition, now silently becomes 5000ms / 2000ms respectively, with no warning — the operator's explicit configuration is discarded and replaced by the default.

findings.title: Do not reject configured 0 runner grace/give-up durations
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs previously accepted 0 (parsed >= 0), so NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 / NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 produced setTimeout(..., 0): SIGTERM is followed by an immediate SIGKILL at src/shared/runner-process.ts:124, and the give-up resolve fires immediately at src/shared/runner-process.ts:123. The new guard parsed > 0 makes 0 fail the ternary, so those env values are silently replaced by the fallbacks (5000 and 2000 at src/shared/runner-process.ts:5 and :9). The knob can no longer express 'no grace period', and a deployment that relied on 0 now waits up to ~7s longer before the promise settles, with no error or warning that its setting was ignored.

findings.title: Honor explicit 0 for runner grace/give-up durations
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing the acceptance predicate from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0` means an explicit zero config value is now treated as invalid and silently replaced by fallbackMs. Substitute the real values: `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` previously yielded RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 so the SIGKILL grace timer fired immediately @src/shared/runner-process.ts:124; it now yields 5000, forcing a 5s wait. Likewise `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` previously yielded RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 so the give-up timer finished immediately @src/shared/runner-process.ts:123, and now yields 2000, forcing a 2s wait. An operator who deliberately sets 0 to skip these waits silently gets the default delay instead, i.e. the configured behavior is overridden without any signal. The prior `>= 0` guard explicitly admitted 0, so this narrows an already-supported value rather than rejecting a nonsensical one.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed backstop collected changed files not present in any mapped hotspot and pushed a tail hotspot so they were still deep-reviewed (comment: 'never silently skip a changed file'). With it gone, reviewLarge iterates only the returned hotspots (bounded by MAX_HOTSPOTS=6), so any changed file the map pass did not assign to a surface is now never deep-reviewed. The critic only receives patchStat, so nothing else covers those files — their diff is silently unreviewed and bugs in them can pass the gate.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously each successful deep pass appended res.residual_risks to a residuals array that was placed into candidateMerged.residual_risks for the critic. The new code no longer collects res.residual_risks and hardcodes residual_risks: [], so deep reviewers' residual risks (including blocks:true 'could not verify / not deep-reviewed' signals) never reach the critic or deriveVerdict. A large PR whose deep pass explicitly flagged blocking uncertainty can now yield a passing verdict.

findings.title: Restore large-PR coverage backstop so no changed file is skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The map pass can leave changed files unmapped (the deleted comment acknowledged exactly that: 'files not mapped to a surface'), and hotspots are truncated to MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 at line 93. The deleted backstop block was the only thing that collected uncovered changed files into a tail hotspot so they were still deep-reviewed. With it gone, any large PR whose changed files are not all covered by the surviving hotspots is deep-reviewed only partially, and the returned findings/checked list contains no signal that those files were skipped — the tool can report a clean summary over never-reviewed changes.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks are silently discarded (defaulted to empty)
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep-pass loop no longer collects `res.residual_risks` (the `residuals` array and `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` were removed), and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is now hardcoded to `[]` at line 113. Previously each deep pass's structured residual risks — including entries with `blocks: true` that explicitly gate the verdict — were merged into the candidate the critic receives (previously line 140). Now those signals never reach the critic prompt (line 116) and the returned review, so a hotspot that could not be cleared reports nothing and the verdict can be derived without the blocking uncertainty the deep pass produced.

findings.title: Restore large-review coverage backstop for unmapped files
findings.whyItBreaks: Base appended a tail hotspot containing every changed file not present in a selected hotspot (base lines 96-110), so every changed file received a deep pass. Head now uses only sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS); any changed file the map pass did not assign to a selected surface (or that fell past the 6-hotspot cap) is never deep-reviewed, yet reviewLarge still runs the critic and returns a complete-looking verdict with no indication the file escaped review — exactly the silent skip the removed comment promised never to allow.

findings.title: Restore per-hotspot error handling and residual-risk propagation
findings.whyItBreaks: Base wrapped each deep pass in try/catch: a failure was recorded in `checked`, collected as a `{blocks:true, text:'... not deep-reviewed'}` residual, and the loop continued (base lines 122-132). Head calls normalizeReview(extractJson(runCodex(...))) unguarded, so one hotspot's throw aborts reviewLarge and discards every other hotspot's findings. It also hardcodes `residual_risks: []` in candidateMerged, so the collected `res.residual_risks` (including the base's blocking marker) are no longer passed to the critic via {{FINDINGS}}; the critic — and onward deriveVerdict — can no longer distinguish 'no residual risk' from 'residual risks were dropped', so blocking uncertainty can silently vanish.

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution and focus in large-PR map/deep passes
findings.whyItBreaks: prompts/deep.md:96 ends with `Focus: {{FOCUS}} (if not "(none)", prioritize findings in that area)`, and the removed line was the only place that fills it. After this change the deep prompt is rendered with the raw placeholder `Focus: {{FOCUS}}`, so every deep pass for a large PR loses the user's focus lens and ships a template artifact to the model. The sibling hunk (removed `focus: bundle.focus` at old line 89, now src/core/review.ts:83-89) additionally strips `focus` from mapBundle, so prompts/map.md:37 ("If a `focus` field is set (not null), rank matching surfaces higher...") can never fire. Net effect: the documented `--focus <text>` flag (src/cli/args.ts:57, `README.md:130`) silently stops narrowing large-PR reviews while still working for small PRs — a user-visible regression with no error surfaced anywhere.

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution in large-PR deep prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: prompts/deep.md ends with a literal `Focus: {{FOCUS}}` line (prompts/deep.md:96). The base code substituted it with `bundle.focus ?? "(none)"`; this diff deletes that `.replace`, so every deep pass prompt sent for a hotspot now contains the raw token `{{FOCUS}}` and never the user's focus. The small path (reviewSmall) still JSON-stringifies the whole bundle including `focus`, so large PRs silently lose a directive the small path keeps — a behavioral regression, not a formatting nit.

findings.title: Keep focus in mapBundle so map ranking honors focus
findings.whyItBreaks: prompts/map.md instructs the map pass: "If a `focus` field is set (not null), rank matching surfaces higher" (prompts/map.md:37). The map prompt sees only the hand-picked `mapBundle` JSON, and this diff removes `focus: bundle.focus` (and `deep: bundle.deep`) from it, so the large-PR map pass can no longer rank or even see the user's focus. Prior behavior (base 76d73ff) passed both fields; reviewSmall still passes them. Net effect: setting `focus` is silently ignored for large PRs.

findings.title: formatDuration can render "Xm 60s" after removing the modulo carry
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous code computed totalSeconds first, then derived minutes/seconds from it (seconds = totalSeconds % 60), which guaranteed seconds < 60. The new code computes minutes = Math.floor(ms / 60000) and seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000) independently, so the second component can round up to 60 while minutes stays un-incremented. Concretely, ms = 119500 → minutes = floor(119500/60000) = 1, seconds = round(59500/1000) = 60, producing "1m 60s" in the rendered review stats (used at src/shared/render.ts:75 and src/shared/render.ts:80). Any ms whose remainder is in [59500, 59999] and >= 60000 total triggers this; old code produced "2m 0s". A related but milder case: ms = 59500 → "60s" instead of "1m 0s".

findings.title: formatDuration can emit "1m 60s" / "60s" at rounding boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floored from the raw ms while seconds is independently rounded from the sub-minute remainder, so the remainder can round up to 60 without carrying into minutes. E.g. ms=119_600 -> minutes=1, seconds=round(59.6)=60 -> "1m 60s" (base produced "2m 0s"); ms=59_600 -> minutes=0, seconds=round(59.6)=60 -> "60s", a value the old formatter could never print since minutes>0 was checked on the rounded total. This stat string is rendered into the review output via renderMarkdown (src/shared/render.ts:75, src/shared/render.ts:80).

findings.title: formatDuration can render 60s after seconds rounded independently
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation rounded total seconds before splitting minutes/seconds, so the seconds component could never reach 60 (e.g. 119600ms -> '2m 0s'). The new code computes minutes separately and then rounds the sub-minute remainder, so any duration whose remainder is >= 59.5s yields seconds=60: ms=59600 -> '60s', ms=119600 -> '1m 60s'. This output is user-visible in the rendered PR review stats line (render.ts:75, render.ts:80).
